stages.title: Advanced chess opening theory
stages.hook: Opening theory is a body of knowledge that no one person holds in full, and it keeps being revised. How is it organised, and how should a serious player use it?
explain: Opening theory is the accumulated knowledge about the first moves, built from game results, human analysis and, increasingly, engine analysis. The Encyclopaedia of Chess Openings (ECO) classifies openings into five volumes by letter: A (flank and irregular openings such as 1.c4 and 1.Nf3), B (semi-open games after 1.e4, such as the Sicilian and Caro-Kann), C (open games 1.e4 e5 and the French), D (closed and semi-closed games such as the Queen's Gambit) and E (Indian defences such as the King's Indian and Nimzo-Indian). Within each letter, numbers identify variations; for example the Najdorf Sicilian is in B90-B99 and the Ruy Lopez in C60-C99.

A tabiya is a standard position reached by many move orders and used as a reference point. Move-order flexibility, transpositions and novelties shape modern practice. Players often think in terms of structures (such as the Hedgehog, Maroczy Bind, IQP or Carlsbad) and plans rather than isolated lines, and use engines to test concrete lines to great depth. Theory also changes: lines once thought refuted can be revived with a new idea, and popular lines can be neutralised.

A repertoire is a strategic choice: sharp openings give winning chances but require more memorisation and more risk; solid ones reduce risk but may offer fewer chances; flexible ones keep options open. Good theory work always asks: what are the typical plans and pawn breaks, what endgames arise, and what happens when the opponent deviates?

example.q: Classify by ECO volume: (a) 1.e4 c5 Najdorf, (b) 1.c4 English, (c) 1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6 King's Indian, (d) 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 Ruy Lopez.
steps: 1.e4 c5 is a semi-open game: volume B.
The English (1.c4) is a flank opening: volume A.
The King's Indian is an Indian defence: volume E, and the Ruy Lopez comes from an open game 1.e4 e5: volume C.

stages.title: Grandmaster positional concepts
stages.hook: Grandmasters often explain a move by what it prevents or by which piece it improves, not by what it threatens. What concepts lie behind such quiet moves?
explain: Grandmaster positional play rests on a handful of ideas developed over a century. Steinitz held that advantages should be accumulated and attacks launched only with an advantage. Nimzowitsch (in My System) emphasised prophylaxis, overprotection of key points, restriction of the opponent's pieces and blockade of passed pawns. Petrosian was famous for prophylaxis and exchange sacrifices. Modern writers such as Silman organise play around imbalances: minor pieces, pawn structure, space, material, control of key files or squares, development lead and initiative.

Useful concepts: static advantages (such as a better structure or a bishop pair) that last, versus dynamic ones (such as initiative or development lead) that fade if not used. Piece quality matters more than counting: a bad bishop, a poor knight on the rim, a passive rook. The "worst piece" principle is to improve the worst-placed piece. Colour complexes, outposts and weak squares guide where to put pieces. Space can be an advantage or a liability: a space advantage helps when opponents have fewer places to put their pieces, so the cramped side wants to trade pieces.
Positional thinking is always checked by concrete calculation: a plan that ignores tactics fails. The best players combine the two, switching between general principles and exact variations.

example.q: You have more space and the opponent is cramped. Should you offer or avoid trades?
steps: A cramped side benefits from trades because it has more room afterwards.
So the side with more space usually avoids unnecessary trades.
Instead, maintain tension and improve pieces.
example.a: Avoid unnecessary trades; keep the opponent cramped

stages.title: Complex middlegame strategy
stages.hook: Middlegames seem endless in variety, but strong players reduce them to a few questions. What are those questions?
explain: Complex middlegame strategy involves balancing attack, defence, structure and timing. Key themes: the timing of pawn breaks (a central break such as ...c5 or e4-e5 is correct only when the pieces are ready), the choice between opening and closing the position, the transition to an endgame, and the interplay of material, space and king safety. Opposite-coloured bishops in the middlegame favour the attacker, since the defender cannot challenge the bishop on its colour; in endings they favour the defender.

When kings castle on opposite sides, a race develops: pawn storms against the king and rapid opening of files. Speed and accuracy matter: each tempo counts. When kings castle on the same side, the attack is slower, with piece manoeuvres and sacrifices on the kingside; the defender seeks counterplay in the centre. A central break often refutes a flank attack, because a flank attack is justified only if the centre is closed or stable.

Dynamic assessments use concepts of initiative, tempo and piece activity. A strong planner asks: which side of the board is most promising, which break will change the structure in my favour, and which piece trades help me? The plan is revised when the opponent finds counterplay.

example.q: Kings are castled on opposite sides and you have the first strike. Which is more important: a slow improving move or opening a file against the enemy king?
steps: In opposite-side castling, tempo decides.
Opening files and attacking with pawns takes priority.
So open the file against the king, unless you need one defensive move.
example.a: Open the file; tempo is decisive

stages.title: Advanced defensive techniques
stages.hook: Down material, in a worse position, many players resign too early. What techniques allow a defender to survive or even turn the game?
explain: Advanced defence begins with realism: assess the position honestly, identify the opponent's main threats, and find the most resilient set-up. Principles: eliminate attacking pieces by trading them, keep the king safe by removing or blocking open lines, use counterattack when passive defence will lose, and look for resources such as a perpetual check, a fortress or a stalemate trick.

A perpetual check is a series of checks that the attacker cannot escape, resulting in a draw by repetition. A fortress is a position where the stronger side cannot make progress, such as a wrong-coloured bishop with a rook pawn when the defending king reaches the corner. A stalemate trick forces a draw by leaving the defender with no legal move while not in check. A well-known example: White king on g6, pawn on h6, Black king on h8; if White plays h7 it is stalemate, and White must be careful.

Practical defence also includes psychological methods: complicating the position, setting traps that need accuracy to avoid, and using time pressure. But do not rely on traps; prefer solid resistance with active chances. Know which trades help: when defending, exchange the opponent's most active pieces.

example.q: White king g6, White pawn h6, Black king h8, White to move. Which pawn move is a stalemate?
steps: The pawn on h6 can advance to h7.
After h7, Black's king on h8 has no legal move: g8 is attacked by the pawn, g7 by the king.
Black is not in check, so it is stalemate and the game is drawn.

stages.title: Deep calculation and candidate moves
stages.hook: Of the dozens of legal moves, grandmasters examine only a handful in depth. How do they choose which ones, and how do they avoid missing the winning one?
explain: Deep calculation is a search problem under limits of time and memory. The average position has about 30 to 35 legal moves, so a full search to even four moves each is impossible by hand. A calculator therefore generates candidate moves with a mixture of pattern recognition and systematic checks: all checks, all captures, all threats, all moves that change the pawn structure, and all "quiet" moves that improve the worst piece or restrict the opponent. Candidates are then pruned by quick tests.

Alexander Kotov's method, from "Think Like a Grandmaster", is to list the candidate moves, then analyse each variation once, noting the evaluation, and only then choose. Errors to avoid: going back and forth between lines (loss of time), stopping on an unstable position (a check or capture still pending), forgetting the opponent's best reply, and falling for an attractive but flawed idea. Check for quiet moves: a move such as a king step that removes the opponent's defence (a waiting move) can be the key, as in positions with zugzwang.

Useful aids are the blunder check (does my move leave something hanging or allow a check?), the use of intermediate evaluation points, and visualisation training by playing out lines in the mind. In long variations, evaluate at stable points, remember the chosen line's final position and compare it to the best alternative. If two lines are close, choose the one with less risk, or the one that keeps more options.

example.q: White: Kg5, Qg1. Black: Kh8. White to move. Find a mate in two, which begins with a quiet move.
steps: Direct checks fail: Qg7+ is met by Kxg7 because the white king on g5 does not guard g7.
The quiet Kf6 guards g7 and takes squares away. Black's only move is Kh7 (Qg1 covers g8).
Then Qg7 is mate: the queen is protected by the king.

stages.title: Advanced technical endgames
stages.hook: A single pawn and two kings can still be a deep mathematical problem. What are the technical rules that decide such endings?
explain: Advanced technical endgames require exact knowledge. In king and pawn endings, the key squares and opposition rules give results: with the king on the sixth rank in front of a pawn on the fifth, the attacker wins whoever has the move (this does not hold for a rook pawn). The Vancura position is a drawing technique for the defender in rook endings with a rook pawn: the defending rook attacks the pawn from the side and keeps checking options along the file. Queen against rook is generally a win for the queen, but it needs technique using forks and the skewering of king and rook, and some fortress positions exist. Rook against a minor piece is often a draw with correct defence, because the defender can set up a fortress.

King, bishop and knight against king is a forced win with the right technique, driving the king to a corner of the bishop's colour, with a maximum of 33 moves. Two knights cannot force mate. Opposite-coloured bishops draw even when a pawn or two down. The fifty-move rule says a player can claim a draw if 50 moves by each side pass without a pawn move or capture; in a few endings, tablebase analysis shows that more than 50 moves may be needed to win, but in practice play follows the rules of the event.

Tablebases (from Nalimov to Syzygy) contain perfect results for all positions with up to seven pieces. They have corrected old books, found very long mates, and shown which positions are fortress draws. Humans still study patterns and principles, because tablebases do not explain why and cannot be consulted in a game.

stages.title: Chess engines and computer-assisted analysis
stages.hook: In 1997 a computer beat the world champion in a match. Today a phone engine is stronger than any human. How do engines work, and how should people use them?
explain: A classical engine searches a tree of moves with alpha-beta pruning and an evaluation function. If a position has about 30 legal moves, a search of depth 4 has 30⁴ = 810,000 leaf positions without pruning; alpha-beta pruning can cut the work enormously when moves are well ordered. Modern engines like Stockfish use a very fast search with an efficiently updatable neural network evaluation (NNUE, adopted in 2020). Another approach, shown by AlphaZero (DeepMind, 2017) and followed by Leela Chess Zero, uses a neural network trained by self-play and Monte Carlo tree search. Deep Blue, which beat Garry Kasparov in a match in 1997, searched many millions of positions per second with specialised hardware.

Engine scores are in centipawns: +100 is about one pawn's advantage for White. Scores depend on search depth, and engines have a horizon problem: they can miss consequences beyond the depth. Engines do not explain; they output best lines. Tablebases supply exact results in endings with up to seven pieces.

Good computer-assisted analysis means forming your own opinion first, using the engine to check critical lines and to look for alternatives, studying the ideas behind the engine's moves, and keeping a record of lessons. Engines have changed opening theory and attacking styles, but fair-play rules ban their use during competition.

stages.title: Chess psychology and decision-making
stages.hook: You are winning, but your hand shakes and you stop calculating, and the win slips away. Why does the mind behave this way, and how can players train it?
explain: Chess psychology studies how thinking, emotion and bias affect decisions. Research since De Groot and Chase and Simon found that masters recall real game positions far better than novices by recognising chunks of familiar patterns, but have little advantage with randomly placed pieces. Expertise is therefore largely pattern knowledge built through experience, supported by calculation.

Common biases: confirmation bias (looking only for evidence that supports your plan), anchoring (sticking to your first impression), loss aversion (taking bad risks to avoid a loss), overconfidence, and the Einstellung effect, in which a familiar solution blocks you from seeing a better one. Emotional states like tilt (playing badly after a setback) and time pressure reduce the quality of decisions. Daniel Kahneman's distinction between fast, intuitive "System 1" thinking and slow, deliberate "System 2" thinking is a useful way to talk about the interplay of intuition and calculation.

Practical methods: use a decision routine (blunder check before each move), manage the clock, reset after errors by focusing on the next move, keep physical routines (sleep, food, breaks), and review games to see patterns. Note that evidence that chess training improves general intelligence or school results is mixed and contested; chess is valuable on its own terms as a skill and a pleasure.

stages.title: Championship simulation and annotated game analysis
stages.hook: Imagine you are a finalist in a world championship match. How do you plan twelve games, read an annotated game, and judge a masterpiece?
explain: A championship match is played over a fixed number of classical games, with one point for a win and half a point for a draw. The first to a majority wins; if tied, tiebreaks with faster time controls decide. Strategy therefore includes scheduling: choosing when to take risks, using rest days and preparing specific opening surprises. A 12-game match needs 6.5 points to win outright; a 14-game match needs 7.5.

Annotated game analysis reads a game as a story: the opening choice, the plans each side pursues, the critical moments, the tactics and the technique that convert. One famous example is the "Opera Game", played in Paris in 1858 by Paul Morphy against the Duke of Brunswick and Count Isouard (1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 Bg4 4.dxe5 Bxf3 5.Qxf3 dxe5 6.Bc4 Nf6 7.Qb3 Qe7 8.Nc3 c6 9.Bg5 b5 10.Nxb5 cxb5 11.Bxb5+ Nbd7 12.O-O-O Rd8 13.Rxd7 Rxd7 14.Rd1 Qe6 15.Bxd7+ Nxd7 16.Qb8+ Nxb8 17.Rd8#). It illustrates a lead in development: White's pieces enter the game quickly while Black's remain passive, and the final queen sacrifice leads to a checkmate.

To write annotations, state the ideas rather than only variations: why a move was played, what it threatened, and what the opponent might have done instead. Check every claim concretely, mark critical moments with the usual symbols, and end with a lesson. A simulation of a championship combines all strands of this world: preparation, structure, tactics, endgames, engines, psychology and honest review.
